entries.meaning: Without saying so directly, but understood. ---
examples: By saying nothing, he tacitly agreed to the plan.
The government tacitly approved the deal.
It was tacitly understood that nobody would mention the divorce.
entries.position: mid

entries.meaning: Carefully, so as not to upset or offend anyone. ---
examples: She tactfully changed the subject.
He tactfully pointed out the mistake.
The complaint needs to be handled tactfully.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: In terms of the methods used to win a game, battle, or contest. ---
examples: Tactically, it was a brilliant move.
The coach changed the team tactically at halftime.
The retreat was tactically necessary.
entries.position: front — as a viewpoint; also before adjectives and at the end

entries.meaning: Without fighting back or showing any spirit; in a weak, disappointing way. ---
examples: He tamely accepted the pay cut without a word.
The home team lost tamely in the second half.
After a great first hour, the movie ends tamely.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: Only slightly or indirectly; not about the main point. ---
examples: The question is only tangentially related to the topic.
The book mentions the war only tangentially.
He was tangentially involved in the scandal.
entries.position: before its word — mostly only tangentially related; also end

entries.meaning: In a real, noticeable way that can be seen or measured. ---
examples: Voters want to see their lives tangibly improve.
Crime has fallen tangibly since the program started.
The new policy has not tangibly changed anything yet.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: In a way that makes you want something you cannot quite have. ---
examples: The team came tantalizingly close to winning.
The smell of fresh bread drifted tantalizingly from the kitchen.
The finish line was tantalizingly near.
entries.position: before its word — most often tantalizingly close

entries.meaning: In a sharp, slightly unkind way. ---
examples: 'I didn't ask for your opinion,' she said tartly.
He replied tartly that he had better things to do.
The editorial tartly noted that the mayor was on vacation during the flood.
entries.position: end — usually after said, replied

entries.meaning: In an attractive way that shows good judgment about style. ---
examples: The living room is tastefully decorated.
The scene was handled tastefully.
She was tastefully dressed in a simple black dress.
entries.position: before its word — before participles (tastefully decorated); also end

entries.meaning: In a way that shows bad taste or may offend people. ---
examples: The room was tastelessly decorated in gold and purple.
He joked tastelessly about the accident.
The ad tastelessly used photos from the disaster.
entries.position: end — or before a participle (tastelessly decorated)

entries.meaning: Tautly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The canvas was stretched tautly over the frame.
Her skin was pulled tautly over her cheekbones.
It's a tautly written thriller.
The film is tautly directed and never drags.

senses.head: Stretched tight, with no slack
examples: The canvas was stretched tautly over the frame.
Her skin was pulled tautly over her cheekbones.

senses.head: In a tight, tense style with nothing extra, of a book or film
examples: It's a tautly written thriller.
The film is tautly directed and never drags.

entries.position: end — or before a participle (tautly written)

entries.meaning: While crying or nearly crying. ---
examples: She tearfully thanked everyone who had helped.
The children said goodbye tearfully.
He tearfully admitted his mistake in court.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: In a playful way that makes fun of someone. ---
examples: 'Nice haircut,' he said teasingly.
She teasingly called him 'Professor.'
He poked her teasingly in the ribs.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In terms of technology. ---
examples: Japan is one of the most technologically advanced countries.
Technologically, the car was years ahead of its time.
The plan is technologically possible but very expensive.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (technologically advanced); also front

entries.meaning: In a long, dull, boring way. ---
examples: The meeting dragged on tediously for three hours.
The movie is tediously long.
He explained the rules tediously, one by one.
entries.position: end — or before its word (tediously long)

entries.meaning: In a way that reveals something important. ---
examples: Tellingly, he didn't deny the story.
The company, tellingly, had no comment on the report.
She wrote tellingly about her years in prison.
entries.position: front — as a comment; also mid or end

entries.meaning: Because of a person's natural character. ---
examples: He was temperamentally unsuited to politics.
Temperamentally, the two brothers are complete opposites.
She's temperamentally calm, even under pressure.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (temperamentally unsuited); also front

entries.meaning: In a way that makes you want something. ---
examples: A plate of cookies sat temptingly on the table.
The beach is temptingly close to the hotel.
The shoes were temptingly priced at $20.
entries.position: end — or before its word (temptingly close)

entries.meaning: Firmly and with determination, without letting go. ---
examples: She fought tenaciously for her patients.
The ivy clings tenaciously to the wall.
The old man held on tenaciously to his land.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Gently and with love. ---
examples: He kissed her tenderly on the forehead.
She tenderly wrapped the baby in a blanket.
The nurse tenderly cleaned the wound.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: By ten times. ---
examples: Sales have increased tenfold since 2020.
The town's population grew tenfold in a decade.
The value of the painting has risen almost tenfold.
entries.position: end — after verbs of growth and change

entries.meaning: In a nervous, worried way. ---
examples: We waited tensely for the results.
The two men faced each other tensely.
She sat tensely on the edge of her chair.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Tentatively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The meeting is tentatively scheduled for Friday.
They've tentatively agreed to sell the house.
She smiled tentatively at the new neighbors.
He tentatively raised his hand.

senses.head: As a plan that is not yet final
examples: The meeting is tentatively scheduled for Friday.
They've tentatively agreed to sell the house.

senses.head: In a hesitant, uncertain way
examples: She smiled tentatively at the new neighbors.
He tentatively raised his hand.

entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: Only weakly or slightly, of a link or hold. ---
examples: The two cases are only tenuously connected.
He's clinging tenuously to his lead in the polls.
The movie is tenuously based on a true story.
entries.position: before its word — before participles (tenuously connected); also end

entries.meaning: Without much interest or enthusiasm. ---
examples: Investors reacted tepidly to the news.
The audience applauded tepidly at the end.
Critics tepidly received the sequel.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: Terminally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her father is terminally ill with cancer.
The hospice cares for terminally ill patients.
The show is terminally boring.
My brother is terminally lazy.

senses.head: With a disease that cannot be cured and will cause death
examples: Her father is terminally ill with cancer.
The hospice cares for terminally ill patients.

senses.head: Hopelessly, as a joking exaggeration
examples: The show is terminally boring.
My brother is terminally lazy.

entries.position: before its word — mostly terminally ill

entries.meaning: Extremely; very — usually in a good sense. ---
examples: She's terrifically talented and very modest about it.
The new restaurant has been doing terrifically well.
It was a terrifically exciting game.
entries.position: before its word — terrifically talented; end in the manner sense

entries.meaning: In a brief, unfriendly way, using very few words. ---
examples: "No comment," the senator said tersely.
She replied tersely to my long email.
The company issued a tersely worded statement.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs, especially verbs of speaking and writing

entries.meaning: In an irritated, impatient way. ---
examples: "I heard you the first time," he said testily.
The coach answered reporters' questions testily after the loss.
She tapped her pen testily on the desk.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In other words; used to explain or correct what was just said. ---
examples: We'll meet next week, that is to say, on Tuesday.
He's a vegan, that is to say, he eats no animal products.
The results were mixed; that is to say, not very good.
entries.type: linking — introduces a more exact restatement
entries.position: front — of the restatement, or mid between commas
entries.modifies: a clause or phrase that explains what came before
entries.form: shortened to that is, written i.e.

entries.meaning: At all; even slightly, in negatives and questions. ---
examples: I'm not the least bit worried.
She didn't seem the least bit surprised.
Are you the least bit interested in what I think?
entries.type: degree — at all, in negatives and questions
entries.position: before its word — an adjective, after not

entries.meaning: In the opposite order, direction or relation. ---
examples: I thought she was helping him, but it was the other way around.
You put the batteries in the other way around.
The dog doesn't walk me; it's the other way around.
entries.type: manner — in the reverse order or relation
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: a clause describing an order or relation
entries.contrast: Russian наоборот has three English equivalents: the other way around (the reverse is true), vice versa (and the reverse too) and on the contrary (you are wrong, the opposite is true). “Are you tired?” “On the contrary!” not “The other way around!”

entries.meaning: Theatrically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He sighed theatrically and rolled his eyes.
She clutched her chest theatrically when she saw the bill.
The villain laughed theatrically as he left the stage.
Theatrically, the production is a triumph.
The script is strong, but theatrically it doesn't quite work.

senses.head: In an exaggerated way that is meant to attract attention
examples: He sighed theatrically and rolled his eyes.
She clutched her chest theatrically when she saw the bill.
The villain laughed theatrically as he left the stage.

senses.head: In terms of the theater or of staging a play
examples: Theatrically, the production is a triumph.
The script is strong, but theatrically it doesn't quite work.

entries.position: end — in the manner sense; front with a comma in the viewpoint sense
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense; not gradable in the viewpoint sense
entries.modifies: verbs; clauses in the viewpoint sense

entries.meaning: In terms of themes or subjects. ---
examples: The three novels are thematically linked.
Thematically, the album deals with loss and recovery.
The exhibit is organized thematically rather than by date.
entries.position: before its word — thematically linked; also front with a comma or end

entries.meaning: On the other hand; used to add a point against what was just said. ---
examples: The car is expensive. Then again, it'll last for years.
He might come, but then again, he might not.
I didn't love the movie, but then again, I'm not a fan of horror.
entries.position: front — often after but
entries.contrast: Despite again, it does not mean one more time. But then again, … weighs a second point against the first.

entries.meaning: In terms of religious belief and theology. ---
examples: The church is theologically conservative.
Theologically, the two groups have little in common.
Her argument is theologically sound.
entries.position: before its word — theologically conservative; also front with a comma

entries.meaning: In a way that treats an illness or helps a person heal. ---
examples: The drug is used therapeutically for chronic pain.
A dose can be therapeutically effective and still cause side effects.
Many people find that gardening works therapeutically for stress.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (therapeutically effective)

entries.meaning: Thereabouts has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The house was built in 1920 or thereabouts.
The repair will cost $500 or thereabouts.
They live in Tulsa or somewhere thereabouts.
The accident happened on Route 9 or thereabouts.

senses.head: Approximately — near the number, amount or time just mentioned
examples: The house was built in 1920 or thereabouts.
The repair will cost $500 or thereabouts.

senses.head: Near the place just mentioned
examples: They live in Tulsa or somewhere thereabouts.
The accident happened on Route 9 or thereabouts.

entries.position: end — almost always after or: in 1990 or thereabouts
entries.modifies: a number, time or place just mentioned
entries.form: there + about + adverbial -s; thereabout is a rarer variant

entries.meaning: After that time; from then on. ---
examples: He retired in 2010 and died shortly thereafter.
The first payment is due in May, with monthly payments thereafter.
Thereafter, the town grew quickly.
entries.position: end — also front, and after shortly or soon (shortly thereafter)

entries.meaning: As a result of that action. ---
examples: The company cut prices, thereby attracting new customers.
By signing the contract, she thereby accepted its terms.
Exercise lowers blood pressure, thereby reducing the risk of stroke.
entries.position: mid — usually before an -ing form (thereby reducing…)
entries.modifies: clauses — gives the result of the action just described

entries.meaning: In that place, document or matter. ---
examples: Therein lies the problem.
Read the contract and the terms contained therein.
The school's rules, and the penalties described therein, apply to every student.
entries.type: place — in that thing or matter
entries.position: end — front only in therein lies…

entries.meaning: Of it or of that — referring to something just mentioned. ---
examples: He was judged on his experience, or lack thereof.
The landlord may keep the deposit or any part thereof.
She pointed out the evidence, or rather the absence thereof.
entries.type: linking — refers back to something just mentioned (of it, of that)
entries.position: after its word — or lack thereof
entries.form: there + of — formal and legal; everyday English uses it mostly in or lack thereof

entries.meaning: In terms of heat, or by means of heat. ---
examples: The new windows are thermally efficient.
The pipes are thermally insulated to keep them from freezing.
The metal parts expand thermally as the engine warms up.
entries.position: before its word — thermally insulated; also end

entries.meaning: In a thick layer, or densely. ---
examples: Spread the frosting on thick.
Complaints came in thick and fast after the price increase.
Cut the bread a little thicker for toast.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective thick
entries.contrast: The flat adverb is informal and mostly fixed: spread it thick, thick and fast, lay it on thick (to exaggerate or flatter too much). In careful writing use thickly. In a thick book, thick is an adjective.

entries.meaning: Thickly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Butter the bread thickly.
The hills are thickly wooded.
Snow lay thickly on the roofs.
"I'm sorry," he said thickly, fighting back tears.
She spoke thickly through her cold.

senses.head: In a thick layer, or close together in large numbers
examples: Butter the bread thickly.
The hills are thickly wooded.
Snow lay thickly on the roofs.

senses.head: In a low, unclear voice, because of emotion, illness or drink
examples: "I'm sorry," he said thickly, fighting back tears.
She spoke thickly through her cold.

entries.position: end — also before a participle (thickly wooded)

entries.meaning: In thin slices or a thin layer. ---
examples: Slice the onions thin.
Roll the dough a little thinner this time.
You're spreading yourself too thin with three jobs.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective thin
entries.contrast: The flat adverb is informal and mostly fixed: slice it thin, spread yourself too thin. In careful writing use thinly. In a thin book, thin is an adjective.

entries.meaning: Thinly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Slice the cucumber thinly.
Apply the paint thinly and let it dry.
The area is thinly populated.
It was a thinly veiled threat.
The meeting was thinly attended.

senses.head: In thin slices or a thin layer
examples: Slice the cucumber thinly.
Apply the paint thinly and let it dry.

senses.head: With only a little of something — few people, little cover, or little effort to hide
examples: The area is thinly populated.
It was a thinly veiled threat.
The meeting was thinly attended.

entries.position: end — after the verb (slice it thinly); before its word in the degree sense (thinly populated)

entries.meaning: Third has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Third, the plan costs too much.
First, it's cheap; second, it's fast; and third, it's safe.
She finished third in the marathon.
Our team came in third this year.

senses.head: In the third place in a list of points
examples: Third, the plan costs too much.
First, it's cheap; second, it's fast; and third, it's safe.

senses.head: In third position in a race, contest or ranking
examples: She finished third in the marathon.
Our team came in third this year.

entries.position: front or end — Third, …; came in third
entries.modifies: clauses; verbs such as finish, come in, rank
entries.form: the ordinal third used as an adverb — also thirdly

entries.meaning: Used to introduce the third point in a list. ---
examples: Thirdly, we need more volunteers.
Firstly, it's too expensive; secondly, it's too slow; and thirdly, nobody asked for it.
Thirdly, the report ignores the cost of maintenance.
entries.type: linking — introduces the third point in a list
entries.position: front — at the start of the sentence, usually with a comma
entries.contrast: American writers often prefer third to thirdly; both are correct, but keep the series consistent: first, second, third or firstly, secondly, thirdly.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are very thirsty or eager for something. ---
examples: The dog lapped thirstily at the bowl.
He drank the cold water thirstily.
The dry soil soaked up the rain thirstily.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Thoughtfully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She looked at him thoughtfully before answering.
He rubbed his chin thoughtfully.
The hotel had thoughtfully left a map in our room.
The house is thoughtfully designed for wheelchair users.

senses.head: In a quiet, serious way, while thinking
examples: She looked at him thoughtfully before answering.
He rubbed his chin thoughtfully.

senses.head: In a kind or careful way that shows you have thought about other people's needs
examples: The hotel had thoughtfully left a map in our room.
The house is thoughtfully designed for wheelchair users.

entries.position: end — also mid, and before a participle (thoughtfully designed)

entries.meaning: Without thinking about the results or about other people. ---
examples: He thoughtlessly parked in front of our driveway.
She spoke thoughtlessly and hurt her friend's feelings.
People toss trash thoughtlessly out of their car windows.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: In a way that suggests harm or danger. ---
examples: The dog growled threateningly.
He stepped threateningly toward me.
Dark clouds gathered threateningly over the hills.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Three times as much or as many. ---
examples: Sales have increased threefold since 2019.
The price of eggs rose almost threefold in a year.
For smokers, the risk grows threefold.
entries.position: end — after a verb of change (grew threefold)
entries.form: three + -fold — also an adjective (a threefold increase)

entries.meaning: Carefully, without wasting money. ---
examples: They lived thriftily and saved for retirement.
She shops thriftily, always checking the sale racks first.
The apartment was thriftily furnished with secondhand pieces.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Completely, in every part or way. ---
examples: She's a New Yorker through and through.
We were soaked through and through.
I know this city through and through.
entries.position: after its word — after a noun, or at the end
entries.modifies: nouns of identity (a New Yorker), verbs like soaked, know

entries.meaning: Throughout has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The house has been painted white throughout.
The hotel offers free Wi-Fi throughout.
The movie was sad, but the kids laughed throughout.
He stayed calm throughout.

senses.head: In every part of a place or thing
examples: The house has been painted white throughout.
The hotel offers free Wi-Fi throughout.

senses.head: During the whole time of an event
examples: The movie was sad, but the kids laughed throughout.
He stayed calm throughout.

entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Most often a preposition (throughout the country, throughout the year). It is an adverb only when no noun follows (painted white throughout).

entries.meaning: Up to this point in time. ---
examples: Thus far, no one has claimed responsibility.
The results thus far are encouraging.
The company has thus far refused to comment.
entries.position: front or end — mid with the present perfect
entries.contrast: A formal so far, common in news and reports; in conversation say so far.

entries.meaning: In this way; like this — informal and often humorous. ---
examples: The steps should be written thusly: ingredients first, then directions.
He explained his theory thusly.
Fold the napkin thusly, and it will look like a swan.
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Many editors call thusly nonstandard or jokey, because thus is already an adverb. In careful writing use thus or like this.

entries.meaning: In a neat and orderly way. ---
examples: Her sweaters were tidily folded in the drawer.
Please stack the chairs tidily against the wall.
The story wraps up a little too tidily at the end.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (tidily folded)

entries.meaning: Tightly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She held her son's hand tightly.
Make sure the lid is tightly closed.
He shut his eyes tightly.
The crowd was tightly packed into the square.
Access to the building is tightly controlled.

senses.head: Firmly and securely, so that something does not move or open
examples: She held her son's hand tightly.
Make sure the lid is tightly closed.
He shut his eyes tightly.

senses.head: Closely, with little space or freedom
examples: The crowd was tightly packed into the square.
Access to the building is tightly controlled.

entries.position: end — also before a participle (tightly packed)
entries.contrast: tight is also an adverb, but only in informal set phrases (hold tight, sleep tight, shut tight). tightly works everywhere and is the only choice before a participle (tightly packed, not tight packed).

entries.meaning: Repeatedly; many times. ---
examples: I've warned him time and again.
Time and again, the team has proven the critics wrong.
She makes the same mistake time and time again.
entries.position: front or end
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: In a shy, nervous way, without confidence. ---
examples: The girl timidly raised her hand.
He knocked timidly on the office door.
"Can I come in?" she asked timidly.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are tired. ---
examples: She smiled tiredly and sat down.
He rubbed his eyes tiredly.
"Let's talk about it tomorrow," he said tiredly.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: With great effort, for a long time, without stopping. ---
examples: She worked tirelessly to raise money for the shelter.
Firefighters worked tirelessly through the night.
He has tirelessly campaigned for cleaner air.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: In a boring or annoying way. ---
examples: The speech was tiresomely long.
He talked tiresomely about his golf game.
The jokes soon became tiresomely familiar.
entries.position: before its word — tiresomely long; end after a verb

entries.meaning: To an excessive degree, of a quality that is usually good. ---
examples: My grandmother was generous to a fault.
He's honest to a fault and can't keep a secret.
The staff are polite to a fault.
entries.type: degree — too much of a good quality
entries.position: after its word — right after an adjective
entries.modifies: adjectives of good qualities: generous, honest, loyal

entries.meaning: Largely; in many ways. ---
examples: Our success depends to a great extent on the weather.
To a great extent, the report is accurate.
Prices are set, to a large extent, by demand.
entries.position: front or end — also mid between commas
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: Less than something else that was mentioned. ---
examples: The storm hit Florida and, to a lesser extent, Georgia.
Kids, and to a lesser extent adults, love the game.
The same is true, to a lesser extent, of smaller cities.
entries.type: degree — less than the thing just named
entries.position: any position — often between commas before the last item
entries.modifies: the last item in a list or a whole clause

entries.meaning: Every one of them, without exception. ---
examples: The players backed their coach to a man.
The voters, to a man, rejected the plan.
They were, to a man, exhausted after the march.
entries.type: degree — every single one, without exception
entries.position: end — or mid between commas

entries.meaning: Exactly; perfectly. ---
examples: That dress fits you to a T.
The description matched him to a T.
She had his accent down to a T.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Backward and forward; first one way, then the other. ---
examples: The branches swayed to and fro in the wind.
He paced to and fro outside the room.
People hurried to and fro across the square.
entries.type: direction — first one way, then the other
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of movement: walk, swing, rock
entries.contrast: Mostly written and a little old-fashioned; in everyday American speech say back and forth.

entries.meaning: Used to give more exact information. ---
examples: We've been married for ten years, eleven to be precise.
To be precise, the meeting starts at 9:15.
He isn't a doctor; he's a nurse, to be precise.
entries.type: viewpoint — giving a more exact detail
entries.position: front or end — or mid between commas
entries.modifies: a whole clause or a detail

entries.meaning: Admittedly; it is true, though something else matters more. ---
examples: To be sure, the plan has risks, but it's our best option.
The hotel was expensive, to be sure, but worth it.
There are, to be sure, a few problems left.
entries.type: stance — concedes a point before a but
entries.position: front or end — or mid between commas
entries.contrast: Formal; it admits something before arguing the other side, and a but usually follows. It is not to make sure (чтобы убедиться).

entries.meaning: To begin with has 2 distinct senses.
examples: To begin with, we can't afford it.
I don't like the job. To begin with, the hours are terrible.
I didn't like him to begin with, but now we're friends.
Why did you agree to begin with?

senses.head: As the first point or reason
examples: To begin with, we can't afford it.
I don't like the job. To begin with, the hours are terrible.

senses.head: At first; at the start
examples: I didn't like him to begin with, but now we're friends.
Why did you agree to begin with?

entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: In addition; as well. ---
examples: She's smart, funny, and a great cook to boot.
The apartment was tiny and expensive to boot.
He lost his job and his car broke down to boot.
entries.position: end — always last in the clause
entries.modifies: a whole clause, adding one more thing
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with a boot (ботинок) or with booting a computer.

entries.meaning: Up to now; until the present time. ---
examples: To date, no one has claimed responsibility for the attack.
The fund has raised $2 million to date.
This is her best album to date.
entries.русский: на сегодняшний день, до сих пор
entries.position: end — or front with a comma
entries.modifies: a whole clause, usually in the present perfect; a superlative (her best work to date)
entries.contrast: Not up to date (современный, актуальный): the report to date is the report so far, but an up-to-date report is a current one. Like so far, it takes the present perfect.

entries.meaning: Specially for a particular customer, when they ask. ---
examples: All our sandwiches are made to order.
The table was built to order.
He has his suits made to order.
entries.type: manner — to a customer's own request
entries.position: end — after made, built, cooked
entries.contrast: Unrelated to in order to (чтобы). Before a noun it is hyphenated: made-to-order furniture.

entries.meaning: Perfectly; exactly as well as possible. ---
examples: The steak was cooked to perfection.
She played the role to perfection.
The plan worked to perfection.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: With that general meaning, though not in exactly those words. ---
examples: He said he was busy, or something to that effect.
There was a sign to that effect on the door.
She called me a liar, or words to that effect.
entries.русский: в этом духе, примерно такого содержания
entries.position: end — often in something to that effect or words to that effect
entries.modifies: something, words, a statement or sign

entries.meaning: In that respect; as far as that point goes. ---
examples: The plan saves money, and to that extent it's a success.
To that extent, I agree with you.
He was only following orders, and to that extent he's not to blame.
entries.русский: в этом смысле, в этой мере
entries.type: degree — as far as that goes
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: Showing or saying the opposite. ---
examples: Despite rumors to the contrary, the store is staying open.
Unless you hear to the contrary, the meeting is at noon.
There's no evidence to the contrary.
entries.type: manner — saying or showing the opposite
entries.position: after its word — right after a noun like evidence, or at the end
entries.modifies: nouns like evidence, proof, claims; verbs of saying
entries.contrast: To the contrary follows a noun or verb: evidence to the contrary (доказательства обратного). On the contrary opens a reply that rejects what was just said: “Was it boring?” “On the contrary, I loved it.”

entries.meaning: Completely; to the fullest possible degree. ---
examples: Their house is mortgaged to the hilt.
I'll back you to the hilt.
He played the villain to the hilt.
entries.type: degree — completely, as far as possible
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs like mortgage, back, play, borrow

entries.meaning: Exactly, paying attention to every detail. ---
examples: Follow the instructions to the letter.
She obeyed the rules to the letter.
We carried out the plan to the letter.
entries.type: manner — exactly as written or told
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of following, obeying, carrying out

entries.meaning: In a direct, close fight or contest, as equals. ---
examples: The small company went toe-to-toe with the tech giants.
The two candidates stood toe-to-toe in the final debate.
The boxers fought toe-to-toe for twelve rounds.
entries.position: end — mostly in go toe-to-toe with
entries.modifies: verbs such as go, stand, fight
entries.form: toe + to + toe — from boxing; also an adjective (a toe-to-toe battle)

entries.meaning: Fairly; well enough, but not very. ---
examples: He speaks Spanish tolerably well.
The motel was tolerably clean.
The weather stayed tolerably warm all week.
entries.position: before its word — tolerably well

entries.meaning: In a patient way that accepts other people's views, habits or faults. ---
examples: She smiled tolerantly at the children's noise.
He listened tolerantly to his father's old stories.
Good teachers treat students' mistakes tolerantly.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a flat voice that shows no feeling. ---
examples: "He's gone," she said tonelessly.
The officer read out the charges tonelessly.
He answered every question tonelessly, staring at the floor.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Not seriously; jokingly, while seeming to be serious. ---
examples: He suggested, tongue-in-cheek, that we cancel Mondays.
The article was clearly written tongue-in-cheek.
She said it tongue-in-cheek, but some people took her seriously.
entries.position: end — also between commas
entries.form: idiom — also an adjective (a tongue-in-cheek review)

entries.meaning: Very fiercely, with all your strength. ---
examples: Residents fought the new highway tooth and nail.
The two teams battled tooth and nail for the title.
She'll fight tooth and nail to keep her job.
entries.русский: не на жизнь, а на смерть; изо всех сил
entries.position: end — after fight

entries.meaning: On the surface of the body rather than by mouth or injection — a medical use. ---
examples: The cream should be applied topically twice a day.
The drug is used topically to treat acne.
Some antibiotics work better topically than in pill form.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as apply, use, treat

entries.meaning: Upside down, or into a state of confusion. ---
examples: The storm turned the whole campground topsy-turvy.
The news turned all our plans topsy-turvy.
Everything went topsy-turvy when the twins were born.
entries.position: end — mostly after turn or go
entries.modifies: verbs such as turn and go
entries.form: rhyming compound — also an adjective (a topsy-turvy world)

entries.meaning: Tortuously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The road winds tortuously up the mountain.
The river twists tortuously through the valley.
The contract is tortuously complicated.
The bill moved tortuously through Congress for two years.

senses.head: In a winding, twisting way
examples: The road winds tortuously up the mountain.
The river twists tortuously through the valley.

senses.head: In a long, overly complicated way
examples: The contract is tortuously complicated.
The bill moved tortuously through Congress for two years.

entries.position: end — after a verb of movement; before its word in the degree sense (tortuously complicated)
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives in the degree sense
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with torturously (painfully, like torture). tortuously is about twists and complications: a tortuously slow process is slow because it is complicated, while torturously slow means painfully slow. Even native writers mix them up.

entries.meaning: In a way that causes great pain or suffering; painfully. ---
examples: The last hour of the flight passed torturously slowly.
The climb to the summit was torturously steep.
The wait for the test results was torturously long.
entries.position: before its word — torturously slow
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with tortuously (in a winding or overly complicated way). torturously comes from torture; tortuously comes from tortuous, twisting.

entries.meaning: In a way that makes you feel sympathy or tenderness. ---
examples: The film is touchingly honest about grief.
He was touchingly proud of his daughter.
She spoke touchingly about her late husband.
entries.position: before its word — touchingly naive; end after a verb

entries.meaning: According to custom, or to what has usually been done for a long time. ---
examples: Traditionally, the bride's family pays for the wedding.
Turkey is traditionally served at Thanksgiving.
The state has traditionally voted Republican.
entries.position: any position — front with a comma; mid (has traditionally voted); before a participle (traditionally served)

entries.meaning: Tragically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He died tragically young.
The trip ended tragically when their boat sank.
Tragically, none of the passengers survived.
Tragically, the warning came too late.

senses.head: In a very sad way, especially one involving death or suffering
examples: He died tragically young.
The trip ended tragically when their boat sank.

senses.head: Used to say that a fact is very sad
examples: Tragically, none of the passengers survived.
Tragically, the warning came too late.

entries.position: any position — mid or end in the manner sense; front with a comma as a comment (Tragically, …)

entries.meaning: In a calm, peaceful way. ---
examples: The baby slept tranquilly in her crib.
The lake lay tranquilly under the morning mist.
Cows grazed tranquilly in the field.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: As a transitive verb — with a direct object. ---
examples: Grow can be used transitively, as in grow tomatoes.
In this sentence the verb break is used transitively.
Some verbs can be used both transitively and intransitively.
entries.position: end — usually after used
entries.modifies: the verb use and its participle
entries.contrast: The opposite is intransitively: run is used transitively in run a business and intransitively in run fast.

entries.meaning: Transparently has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The city must spend public money transparently.
The charity operates transparently and publishes its accounts online.
His excuse was transparently false.
It was a transparently political move.

senses.head: Openly, so that people can see what is being done
examples: The city must spend public money transparently.
The charity operates transparently and publishes its accounts online.

senses.head: Very obviously — about a lie or a motive that is easy to see through
examples: His excuse was transparently false.
It was a transparently political move.

entries.position: end — in the manner sense; before its word in the degree sense (transparently false)
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives in the degree sense

entries.meaning: Treacherously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The roads were treacherously icy this morning.
The rocks near the shore are treacherously slippery.
He treacherously sold the plans to a rival company.
The general was treacherously murdered by his own officers.

senses.head: In a way that is dangerous, often more than it looks
examples: The roads were treacherously icy this morning.
The rocks near the shore are treacherously slippery.

senses.head: By betraying someone who trusted you
examples: He treacherously sold the plans to a rival company.
The general was treacherously murdered by his own officers.

entries.position: before its word — treacherously icy; mid or end in the betrayal sense
entries.modifies: adjectives; verbs in the betrayal sense

entries.meaning: In a shaky way, because of fear, nervousness or strong emotion. ---
examples: "Is anyone there?" she asked tremulously.
He smiled tremulously through his tears.
Her voice rose tremulously on the last note.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs, especially of speaking and smiling

entries.meaning: In a sharp, clear and forceful way — about criticism or argument. ---
examples: She trenchantly criticized the new policy.
The essay is trenchantly argued.
He wrote trenchantly about corruption in city politics.
entries.position: end — also mid, and before a participle (trenchantly argued)
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking and writing, and participles

entries.meaning: In a way that shows pride and joy at winning or succeeding. ---
examples: She waved the winning ticket triumphantly.
The team returned home triumphantly to a hero's welcome.
"I told you so," he said triumphantly.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: So simply or so slightly that it hardly matters or needs explaining. ---
examples: The fix was trivially easy once we found the bug.
The statement is trivially true.
The two versions differ only trivially.
entries.position: before its word — trivially easy; end after a verb

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you believe someone is honest or will not hurt you. ---
examples: The child looked up at her trustingly.
The puppy followed him trustingly down the street.
She trustingly gave the caller her bank details.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: Truthfully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Please answer the questions truthfully.
He could truthfully say he had never cheated.
Truthfully, I never liked that job.
Truthfully, I have no idea what happened.

senses.head: Honestly; without lying
examples: Please answer the questions truthfully.
He could truthfully say he had never cheated.

senses.head: Used to show that you are giving your honest opinion
examples: Truthfully, I never liked that job.
Truthfully, I have no idea what happened.

entries.position: end — in the manner sense; front with a comma as a stance adverb
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (more truthfully); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.modifies: verbs; clauses as a stance adverb

entries.meaning: Without a clear or pleasant tune. ---
examples: He whistled tunelessly while he worked.
She hummed tunelessly to herself.
The kids sang tunelessly but happily.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as whistle, hum, sing

entries.meaning: Twice as much or as many. ---
examples: The number of applicants increased twofold.
Rents have risen nearly twofold in five years.
The risk of injury rose twofold among older players.
entries.position: end — after a verb of change (rose twofold)
entries.form: two + -fold — more often an adjective (a twofold purpose)

entries.meaning: Typically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The trip typically takes about three hours.
Typically, the store closes at nine.
It was a typically American breakfast of eggs and bacon.
He was typically modest about his success.

senses.head: Usually; in most cases
examples: The trip typically takes about three hours.
Typically, the store closes at nine.

senses.head: In a way that is characteristic of a person, group or thing
examples: It was a typically American breakfast of eggs and bacon.
He was typically modest about his success.

entries.position: mid — also front with a comma; before its word in the 'characteristically' sense
entries.modifies: verbs and clauses; adjectives in the 'characteristically' sense

entries.meaning: In the end, after a long process; or at the most basic level. ---
examples: The project ultimately cost twice as much as planned.
Their marriage ultimately ended in divorce.
Ultimately, the decision is yours.
entries.type: time — in the end; also stance (basically)
entries.position: mid — also front with a comma
entries.contrast: A false friend: it does not mean 'in the form of an ultimatum' (ультимативно). It means 'in the end' or 'at the most basic level'.

entries.meaning: Openly, without embarrassment or apology. ---
examples: The film is unabashedly sentimental.
She is unabashedly proud of her hometown.
He unabashedly admitted he had never read the book.
entries.position: before its word — unabashedly romantic; also mid

entries.meaning: To a degree or in a way that cannot be accepted. ---
examples: Unemployment remains unacceptably high.
The wait times at the clinic are unacceptably long.
He behaved unacceptably at the meeting.
entries.position: before its word — unacceptably high; end after a verb

entries.meaning: In a way that nobody can explain; for some unknown reason. ---
examples: She felt unaccountably sad all day.
The letter was unaccountably delayed.
Unaccountably, the key was back in the drawer.
entries.position: before its word — unaccountably nervous; also mid, or front with a comma

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be changed. ---
examples: The senator is unalterably opposed to the tax increase.
The accident unalterably changed his life.
Their friendship was unalterably damaged by the lawsuit.
entries.position: before its word — unalterably opposed; also mid

entries.meaning: Clearly, in a way that can only be understood one way. ---
examples: The law states unambiguously that the tax applies to everyone.
The results unambiguously support the theory.
Voters rejected the plan unambiguously.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: With everyone agreeing or voting the same way. ---
examples: The board voted unanimously to approve the budget.
The bill passed the Senate unanimously.
Critics unanimously praised her performance.
entries.position: end — also mid
entries.modifies: verbs such as vote, agree, approve

entries.meaning: Used to say that something is true and nobody could disagree. ---
examples: She is unarguably the best player on the team.
Unarguably, the city needs more affordable housing.
It was unarguably a mistake.
entries.position: mid — also front with a comma, and before an adjective

entries.meaning: Openly, without feeling ashamed or embarrassed. ---
examples: The novel is unashamedly romantic.
He cried unashamedly at his daughter's wedding.
The show is unashamedly old-fashioned.
entries.position: before its word — unashamedly romantic; also mid

entries.meaning: In a way that is not pleasant to look at or not appealing. ---
examples: The food was unattractively served on paper plates.
The old mall is unattractively designed, with no windows at all.
He was unattractively smug about his win.
entries.position: before its word — unattractively designed; also end

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be prevented. ---
examples: The flight was unavoidably delayed by the storm.
The doctor was unavoidably detained at the hospital.
On a project this large, some mistakes will unavoidably happen.
entries.русский: неизбежно, по не зависящим от нас причинам
entries.position: mid — also before a participle (unavoidably delayed)

entries.meaning: By surprise, when someone is not ready or expecting it. ---
examples: The early snowstorm caught the city unawares.
The question took her unawares, and she didn't know what to say.
The guards were caught unawares by the attack.
entries.position: end — mostly in catch or take someone unawares
entries.modifies: verbs such as catch and take
entries.form: un- + aware + adverbial -s — not a plural
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with the adjective unaware (I was unaware of the problem). unawares is the adverb (The news caught me unawares).

entries.meaning: To a degree that is too unpleasant or painful to accept. ---
examples: It was unbearably hot in the car.
The music next door was unbearably loud.
The waiting was unbearably painful.
entries.position: before its word — unbearably hot

entries.meaning: Without someone knowing about it — always followed by to. ---
examples: Unbeknownst to her parents, she had dropped out of college.
Unbeknownst to us, the tickets had already sold out.
The company had, unbeknownst to its customers, been selling their data.
entries.type: manner — always with to: without someone's knowledge
entries.position: front — unbeknownst to me, …; also between commas
entries.form: un- + old beknown (known) + -st; unbeknown is a rarer, mostly British variant

entries.meaning: Unbelievably has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The view from the top was unbelievably beautiful.
He's unbelievably rude to waiters.
Unbelievably, nobody was hurt in the crash.
Unbelievably, the store was still open at midnight.

senses.head: Extremely — to a degree that is hard to believe
examples: The view from the top was unbelievably beautiful.
He's unbelievably rude to waiters.

senses.head: Used to say that something is surprising and hard to believe
examples: Unbelievably, nobody was hurt in the crash.
Unbelievably, the store was still open at midnight.

entries.position: before its word — unbelievably good; front with a comma as a comment
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; clauses as a comment

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you cannot believe what you see or hear. ---
examples: She stared unbelievingly at the lottery ticket.
He shook his head unbelievingly when he heard the score.
"You did what?" his mother asked unbelievingly.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as stare, look, ask
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with unbelievably (extremely; surprisingly). She stared unbelievingly describes how she looked; She was unbelievably tired means very tired.

entries.meaning: Without blinking; steadily, without looking away or showing emotion. ---
examples: The cat stared at me unblinkingly.
She looked unblinkingly at the judge.
The documentary looks unblinkingly at life in prison.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as stare, look, watch

entries.meaning: In a strange, surprising way that is hard to explain. ---
examples: She looks uncannily like her grandmother.
His prediction turned out to be uncannily accurate.
The house was uncannily quiet.
entries.position: before its word — uncannily accurate

entries.meaning: Without stopping; continuously. ---
examples: The rain fell unceasingly for three days.
She worked unceasingly to find a cure.
The neighbor's dog barked unceasingly all night.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: Suddenly and rudely, without politeness or any ceremony. ---
examples: He was unceremoniously fired after twenty years with the company.
The bouncer threw them unceremoniously out of the club.
Her old sofa was unceremoniously dumped on the curb.
entries.position: end — also mid, and before a participle (unceremoniously dumped)

entries.meaning: In a way that shows doubt or a lack of confidence. ---
examples: She smiled uncertainly at the stranger.
He stood uncertainly in the doorway.
The toddler walked uncertainly across the room.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: In a way that is not typical of someone or something. ---
examples: He was uncharacteristically quiet at dinner.
The team played uncharacteristically badly.
Uncharacteristically, she forgot my birthday.
entries.position: before its word — uncharacteristically quiet; also front with a comma

entries.meaning: In a way that is hard to understand, see or hear. ---
examples: The instructions were unclearly written.
He spoke so unclearly that nobody understood him.
If you express yourself unclearly, people will guess what you mean.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (unclearly written)

entries.meaning: Uncomfortably has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He shifted uncomfortably in his chair.
She laughed uncomfortably at the joke.
It was uncomfortably hot in the office.
The hurricane came uncomfortably close to the coast.

senses.head: In a way that shows you feel physically uncomfortable or embarrassed
examples: He shifted uncomfortably in his chair.
She laughed uncomfortably at the joke.

senses.head: To an unpleasant or worrying degree
examples: It was uncomfortably hot in the office.
The hurricane came uncomfortably close to the coast.

entries.position: end — in the manner sense; before its word in the degree sense (uncomfortably hot)
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives and adverbs in the degree sense

entries.meaning: Unusually; to an unusual degree. ---
examples: She is an uncommonly gifted pianist.
It's uncommonly warm for February.
He was uncommonly kind to us.
entries.position: before its word — uncommonly good

entries.meaning: Without complaining. ---
examples: She uncomplainingly cared for her sick mother for years.
The soldiers marched uncomplainingly through the rain.
He accepted the extra work uncomplainingly.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: Without changing your ideas or standards to please anyone. ---
examples: The film is uncompromisingly bleak.
She is uncompromisingly honest with her students.
He fought uncompromisingly for workers' rights.
entries.position: before its word — uncompromisingly honest; also end

entries.meaning: In a calm way that shows you are not worried or not interested. ---
examples: He shrugged unconcernedly and went back to his book.
The cat watched unconcernedly as the dog barked at it.
She walked unconcernedly past the long line.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without any conditions or limits. ---
examples: Most parents love their children unconditionally.
The army surrendered unconditionally.
The prisoners were released unconditionally.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as love, support, surrender

entries.meaning: Without knowing it or intending it. ---
examples: She unconsciously touches her hair when she's nervous.
We often copy our parents' habits unconsciously.
He was unconsciously tapping his foot to the music.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: In a way that goes against a country's constitution. ---
examples: The court ruled that the police had acted unconstitutionally.
The law unconstitutionally limits free speech.
Critics say the governor spent the funds unconstitutionally.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be stopped or controlled. ---
examples: She laughed uncontrollably at his joke.
His hands were shaking uncontrollably.
The fire spread uncontrollably through the dry forest.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as shake, cry, laugh, spread

entries.meaning: In a way that is different from what most people do. ---
examples: She dresses unconventionally for a lawyer.
The house is unconventionally designed, with no interior walls.
He was raised unconventionally on a sailboat.
entries.position: end — also before a participle

entries.meaning: In a way that does not make people believe you. ---
examples: "I'm fine," she said unconvincingly.
He argued unconvincingly that the money had been a gift.
The actor played the villain unconvincingly.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without questioning whether something is true or good. ---
examples: Many people uncritically accept what they read online.
The reporter repeated the company's claims uncritically.
Fans praised the sequel uncritically.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: In a way that ignores people's right to vote or have a say. ---
examples: The leader was accused of ruling undemocratically.
The decision was made undemocratically, without a vote.
The party chose its candidate undemocratically.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Used to say that something is certainly true. ---
examples: She is undeniably talented.
Undeniably, the plan has some problems.
The new design is undeniably better than the old one.
entries.position: mid — also front with a comma, and before an adjective

entries.meaning: Under has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The boat hit the rocks and went under.
She took a deep breath and stayed under for a full minute.
Tickets are $10 for kids 12 and under.
Anyone who scores 50 or under has to retake the test.
The patient was put under for the surgery.
He was under for about two hours.

senses.head: Below something, especially below the surface of water
examples: The boat hit the rocks and went under.
She took a deep breath and stayed under for a full minute.

senses.head: Less than a stated number, amount or age
examples: Tickets are $10 for kids 12 and under.
Anyone who scores 50 or under has to retake the test.

senses.head: Unconscious, especially because of an anesthetic
examples: The patient was put under for the surgery.
He was under for about two hours.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as go, stay, put; numbers in and under
entries.contrast: Most often a preposition (under the table). It is an adverb only when no noun follows (The boat went under). go under also means that a business fails.

entries.meaning: Because of the situation; considering what has happened. ---
examples: Under the circumstances, we had no choice.
You did the best you could under the circumstances.
The team played well under the circumstances.
entries.русский: в данных обстоятельствах, в такой ситуации
entries.position: front or end
entries.contrast: Americans say under the circumstances; in the circumstances is more British. Russian при таких обстоятельствах does not become at or by the circumstances.

entries.meaning: Started and now in progress. ---
examples: Work on the new bridge is well under way.
The meeting got under way at ten.
Plans are under way for a new stadium.
entries.type: time — already started and in progress
entries.position: end — after be or get
entries.form: often written as one word, underway

entries.meaning: Underfoot has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The trail was muddy and slippery underfoot.
Dry leaves crunched underfoot as we walked.
I can't cook with the kids underfoot all the time.
The puppy was always underfoot in the kitchen.

senses.head: Under your feet; on the ground you walk on
examples: The trail was muddy and slippery underfoot.
Dry leaves crunched underfoot as we walked.

senses.head: In the way, so that you keep almost stepping on someone
examples: I can't cook with the kids underfoot all the time.
The puppy was always underfoot in the kitchen.

entries.position: end — after the verb or a noun
entries.modifies: verbs of being and moving; nouns (the ground underfoot)

entries.meaning: With the hand kept below the shoulder, swinging up and forward. ---
examples: She tossed the ball underhand to her little brother.
If you're just learning, serve underhand.
He pitched underhand in the office softball game.
entries.position: end — after throw, toss, pitch, serve
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective underhand
entries.contrast: In American English underhand is mostly about throwing (British underarm). The sense 'sneaky, dishonest' is usually the adjective underhanded (an underhanded trick), not this adverb.

entries.meaning: In a secret and dishonest way. ---
examples: The company was accused of acting underhandedly.
He underhandedly took credit for her work.
The deal was pushed through underhandedly, without a public vote.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: In a sympathetic way that shows you understand someone's feelings. ---
examples: She nodded understandingly when I explained why I was late.
The doctor smiled understandingly.
He listened understandingly to all my complaints.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking
entries.modifies: verbs such as nod, smile, listen
entries.contrast: understandingly = with sympathy (с пониманием): She nodded understandingly. understandably = for reasons anyone can see (понятно, что): She was understandably upset.

entries.meaning: In a way that someone or something has not earned. ---
examples: The film was undeservedly ignored at the Oscars.
I feel I was blamed undeservedly.
It's an undeservedly forgotten novel.
entries.position: mid or end — also before its word (undeservedly forgotten)

entries.meaning: In a way that nobody argues with. ---
examples: She is undisputedly the best player on the team.
The diner is undisputedly the most popular place in town.
He was undisputedly the leader of the group.
entries.position: mid — after be, before the phrase it stresses (undisputedly the best)
entries.modifies: noun phrases and superlatives after be

entries.meaning: More than is necessary or reasonable. ---
examples: Don't be unduly worried about the test.
The punishment seemed unduly harsh.
Doctors say there is no reason to be unduly alarmed.
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective or participle
entries.modifies: adjectives and participles, often after a negative (not unduly worried)
entries.form: -ly from undue, with the final e dropped

entries.meaning: In a nervous, worried or uncomfortable way. ---
examples: He shifted uneasily in his chair.
She laughed uneasily and changed the subject.
The two groups live side by side uneasily.
entries.position: end
entries.form: -ly from uneasy, with y becoming i

entries.meaning: Without showing any feelings. ---
examples: She described the accident calmly and unemotionally.
He spoke unemotionally about his divorce.
The judge read the verdict unemotionally.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without ever stopping or running out. ---
examples: My grandmother was unendingly patient with us.
The debate seemed to go on unendingly.
I find the subject unendingly fascinating.
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective (unendingly patient); also end

entries.meaning: Without interest or excitement. ---
examples: The kids agreed unenthusiastically to clean their rooms.
The audience clapped unenthusiastically at the end.
"Sure," she said unenthusiastically.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In amounts or ways that are not the same or not fair. ---
examples: Wealth is distributed very unequally in this country.
The work was divided unequally between the two teams.
Men and women are still paid unequally for the same job.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (unequally divided)

entries.meaning: Clearly and firmly, leaving no doubt. ---
examples: The senator unequivocally denied the charges.
