entries.position: end — usually after a verb of looking
entries.modifies: verbs such as stare, look, smile

entries.meaning: Vaguely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I vaguely remember meeting him at a party.
She waved vaguely toward the back of the store.
He answered vaguely when I asked about his plans.
His face looked vaguely familiar.
I felt vaguely uneasy about the whole thing.

senses.head: Not clearly or exactly
examples: I vaguely remember meeting him at a party.
She waved vaguely toward the back of the store.
He answered vaguely when I asked about his plans.

senses.head: Slightly; a little
examples: His face looked vaguely familiar.
I felt vaguely uneasy about the whole thing.

entries.position: mid or end — also before its word (vaguely familiar)

entries.meaning: Without success; in vain. ---
examples: He searched vainly for his keys.
She tried vainly to hide her disappointment.
Rescuers worked vainly through the night.
entries.position: mid or end
entries.modifies: verbs such as try, search, hope
entries.contrast: The adjective vain means both 'useless' and 'conceited' (тщеславный), but vainly nearly always means 'in vain, without success'.

entries.meaning: Bravely and with great effort, often against the odds. ---
examples: Firefighters fought valiantly to save the house.
Our team played valiantly but lost in overtime.
She struggled valiantly against the disease.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as fight, try, struggle

entries.meaning: In a way that is legally or logically correct. ---
examples: The contract was validly signed by both parties.
Only validly registered voters may cast a ballot.
You can't validly compare the two studies.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (validly signed)

entries.meaning: So little that it almost does not exist. ---
examples: The chances of that happening are vanishingly small.
Cases like his are vanishingly rare.
The number of voters who changed their minds was vanishingly small.
entries.position: before its word — almost always small, rare or few
entries.modifies: adjectives of size and number: small, rare, few, thin

entries.meaning: In different ways, by different people or at different times. ---
examples: He has been variously described as a genius and a fraud.
The crowd was variously estimated at 5,000 to 10,000 people.
The town's name is variously spelled on old maps.
entries.position: mid — before a participle (variously described as)
entries.modifies: past participles of describing, estimating and naming

entries.meaning: Very much; to a very great degree. ---
examples: The two cities are vastly different.
Her new job is vastly better paid than the old one.
The software has vastly improved since last year.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and comparatives (vastly different, vastly better); mid before a verb (vastly improved)
entries.modifies: adjectives, comparatives and verbs of change

entries.meaning: With very strong feeling, especially in disagreeing. ---
examples: He vehemently denied the accusations.
Local residents are vehemently opposed to the new highway.
She argued vehemently against the plan.
entries.position: mid or end — before verbs of denying and opposing (vehemently denied)
entries.modifies: verbs of denying, opposing, arguing and objecting

entries.meaning: In a way that shows a wish to get revenge. ---
examples: He smiled vengefully as his rival lost the election.
The fired employee acted vengefully and deleted the company's files.
She glared vengefully at the referee.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: With bitter hatred or spite. ---
examples: "Get out of my house," she said venomously.
He wrote venomously about his former business partners.
The two candidates attacked each other venomously.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, writing and looking

entries.meaning: Verbally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The referee was verbally abused by angry fans.
He verbally attacked the reporter during the press conference.
She never hit anyone, but she was verbally aggressive.
We agreed verbally, but nothing was signed.
The warning was given verbally before the written notice arrived.

senses.head: With words rather than actions or physical force
examples: The referee was verbally abused by angry fans.
He verbally attacked the reporter during the press conference.
She never hit anyone, but she was verbally aggressive.

senses.head: In speech rather than in writing
examples: We agreed verbally, but nothing was signed.
The warning was given verbally before the written notice arrived.

entries.position: end — or mid before a verb or participle (verbally abused)

entries.meaning: In exactly the same words. ---
examples: She repeated his words verbatim.
The student copied whole paragraphs verbatim from a website.
I'm quoting the email verbatim here.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of quoting, copying and repeating
entries.form: from Latin; the same form is an adjective (a verbatim record)

entries.meaning: Using more words than needed. ---
examples: He writes verbosely, and his reports are hard to follow.
The instructions were verbosely written and confusing.
She explained the rule verbosely when one sentence would have done.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of writing, speaking and explaining

entries.meaning: Straight up and down, at a right angle to the ground. ---
examples: Cut the pepper in half vertically.
Hold the bottle vertically while you pour.
The title runs vertically down the side of the page.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: To a great degree; a lot. ---
examples: Thank you very much.
We enjoyed the concert very much.
I very much doubt he'll show up.
entries.position: end — after the object; mid before hope, doubt, appreciate
entries.modifies: verbs, comparatives (very much better), some past participles
entries.contrast: Very alone cannot modify a verb: I like it very much, not I very like it. Very much goes after the object, not between the verb and object: not I like very much jazz. Mid position works only with a few verbs: I very much hope so.

entries.meaning: Very well has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She speaks Spanish very well.
I don't know him very well.
The interview went very well.
That may very well be true.
The price could very well go up next year.

senses.head: In a very good or skillful way
examples: She speaks Spanish very well.
I don't know him very well.
The interview went very well.

senses.head: Quite possibly, after may, might or could
examples: That may very well be true.
The price could very well go up next year.

entries.position: end — mid after may, might, could
entries.modifies: verbs; modal verbs in may very well
entries.contrast: Alone at the start of a reply, Very well is a formal OK (хорошо, ладно) and sounds stiff in America. I'm very well uses well as an adjective (healthy).

entries.meaning: By watching or hearing about someone else's experiences instead of having them yourself. ---
examples: Some parents live vicariously through their kids.
I travel vicariously by following my friend's trip online.
We enjoyed the concert vicariously through her photos.
entries.position: end — most often in live vicariously through
entries.modifies: verbs like live, enjoy, experience, travel

entries.meaning: With the two things just mentioned the other way around. ---
examples: I help her with math, and vice versa.
You can drive from Boston to New York or vice versa.
Cats often dislike dogs, and vice versa.
entries.position: end — usually after and or or
entries.modifies: a statement whose two parts can be swapped
entries.contrast: Use it only when the same statement is true with the two parts swapped: Cats hate dogs and vice versa. For a plain reversal say the other way around; to reject what was said, on the contrary. All three are Russian наоборот.

entries.meaning: In a cruel, violent or very hostile way. ---
examples: The dog viciously attacked a mail carrier.
He was viciously beaten and left on the street.
Critics attacked the movie viciously.
entries.position: end — or mid before a participle (viciously attacked)

entries.meaning: As a winner; in a way that shows you have won. ---
examples: The team returned home victoriously.
She raised her fist victoriously as she crossed the finish line.
The army marched victoriously into the capital.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Carefully watching for danger or problems. ---
examples: Security guards watched the crowd vigilantly.
Parents should monitor their kids' screen time vigilantly.
The border is vigilantly patrolled.
entries.position: end — or mid before a participle (vigilantly guarded)
entries.modifies: verbs of watching, guarding and checking

entries.meaning: With a lot of energy, force or determination. ---
examples: Stir the mixture vigorously for two minutes.
The company vigorously denied any wrongdoing.
She nodded vigorously when I asked if she wanted to come.
entries.position: end — or mid before a verb (vigorously denied)
entries.modifies: verbs of physical action, and of denying, defending and opposing

entries.meaning: In a way meant to hurt someone who you think has wronged you. ---
examples: The boss treated him vindictively after he complained.
She vindictively posted his private messages online.
They acted vindictively, not out of any sense of justice.
entries.position: end — or mid before a verb

entries.meaning: Violently has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The protest ended violently.
He was violently attacked in the parking lot.
The prisoners reacted violently to the new rules.
She was violently ill after eating the shrimp.
The whole plane shook violently.
They disagree violently about politics.

senses.head: With physical force that hurts or damages
examples: The protest ended violently.
He was violently attacked in the parking lot.
The prisoners reacted violently to the new rules.

senses.head: Very strongly, suddenly or severely
examples: She was violently ill after eating the shrimp.
The whole plane shook violently.
They disagree violently about politics.

entries.position: end — or mid before a participle (violently attacked); before its word for degree (violently ill)
entries.modifies: verbs, past participles and a few adjectives (ill, opposed)

entries.meaning: With strong hatred or bitter hostility. ---
examples: The pamphlet was virulently anti-immigrant.
Both parties virulently attacked the report.
She has virulently opposed the plan from the start.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (virulently racist); mid or end with verbs
entries.modifies: adjectives of hostility and verbs of attacking and opposing

entries.meaning: In a deep, instinctive way that you feel in your body rather than think through. ---
examples: I reacted viscerally to the photos from the war.
Fans respond viscerally to his music.
The movie is viscerally frightening.
entries.position: mid or end — before adjectives and verbs (viscerally frightening, react viscerally)
entries.modifies: verbs of reacting and feeling; adjectives of emotion

entries.meaning: In a way that other people can clearly see. ---
examples: She was visibly upset when she left the meeting.
He was visibly shaken by the news.
Her father had visibly aged since the last time I saw him.
entries.position: mid — before participles and adjectives (visibly shaken)
entries.modifies: past participles and adjectives of feeling; verbs of change
entries.contrast: False friend: visibly means 'in a way you can see' (заметно, явно). Russian видимо in the sense 'apparently' is apparently or evidently: Видимо, он устал is Apparently he was tired, not Visibly he was tired.

entries.meaning: Extremely; in a way that is essential. ---
examples: It's vitally important that you take this medicine every day.
Clean water is vitally needed in the region.
Teachers are vitally interested in the outcome of the vote.
entries.position: before its word — almost always vitally important
entries.modifies: adjectives and participles: important, necessary, needed, interested

entries.meaning: Very clearly and in a lot of detail; with bright colors. ---
examples: I vividly remember the day we met.
The book describes life on the frontier vividly.
The birds were vividly colored.
entries.position: mid or end — before remember and recall; after other verbs
entries.modifies: verbs of remembering and describing; participles like colored

entries.meaning: Vocally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Parents have been vocally opposed to the new schedule.
She has spoken out vocally against the war.
Vocally, the song is very demanding.
The new album is vocally stronger than her last one.

senses.head: Openly and loudly, in expressing an opinion
examples: Parents have been vocally opposed to the new schedule.
She has spoken out vocally against the war.

senses.head: In terms of the voice or singing
examples: Vocally, the song is very demanding.
The new album is vocally stronger than her last one.

entries.position: any position — mid before a participle (vocally opposed); front with a comma for the singing sense
entries.modifies: verbs of supporting and opposing; whole clauses

entries.meaning: Loudly and forcefully, in expressing an opinion. ---
examples: Fans complained vociferously about the referee's call.
The senator vociferously opposed the bill.
They argued vociferously for hours.
entries.position: mid or end
entries.modifies: verbs of complaining, arguing, opposing and supporting

entries.meaning: Because you choose to, not because you are forced or paid. ---
examples: He left the company voluntarily.
The driver voluntarily surrendered to police.
Nobody is paid here — everyone works voluntarily.
entries.position: end — or mid before the verb

entries.meaning: With a huge appetite, for food or for things like books and news. ---
examples: She reads voraciously — two or three books a week.
The kids ate voraciously after the game.
He follows the news voraciously.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Deep enough to reach your waist. ---
examples: We waded waist-deep into the river.
The fishermen stood waist-deep in the cold water.
The soldiers marched waist-deep through the swamp.
entries.position: end — after stand, wade, sink, usually before in or into
entries.modifies: verbs of standing and moving in water, snow or mud
entries.form: waist + deep; the same form is an adjective (waist-deep water)

entries.meaning: In a pale, weak or tired way, most often about a smile. ---
examples: She smiled wanly from her hospital bed.
He waved wanly as the bus pulled away.
The winter sun shone wanly through the clouds.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Deliberately, without any reason, and with no care for the harm done. ---
examples: The vandals wantonly destroyed the benches in the park.
Soldiers were accused of wantonly killing civilians.
He wantonly ignored the safety of his passengers.
entries.position: mid or end — usually before the verb
entries.modifies: verbs of destroying, killing and disregarding

entries.meaning: Carefully, because you do not trust someone or expect danger. ---
examples: The cat watched the dog warily.
She eyed the stranger warily.
Investors are warily watching interest rates.
entries.position: end — or mid before the verb
entries.modifies: verbs of watching, approaching and reacting
entries.contrast: Do not mix up warily (настороженно, from wary) and wearily (устало, from weary): The cat watched the dog warily, but He climbed the stairs wearily.

entries.meaning: Warmly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Our hosts welcomed us warmly.
She smiled warmly at the children.
The movie was warmly received at the festival.
Dress warmly — it's below zero out there.
The baby was warmly wrapped in a blanket.

senses.head: In a friendly, kind way
examples: Our hosts welcomed us warmly.
She smiled warmly at the children.
The movie was warmly received at the festival.

senses.head: So as to keep warm
examples: Dress warmly — it's below zero out there.
The baby was warmly wrapped in a blanket.

entries.position: end — or mid before a participle (warmly received)
entries.modifies: verbs of greeting, thanking and smiling; dress, wrap
entries.contrast: In casual American speech dress warm is common, but dress warmly is the standard form in writing.

entries.meaning: In a way that uses more money, time or resources than needed. ---
examples: The agency spent the money wastefully.
We use water very wastefully in this town.
Tons of food are wastefully thrown away every day.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without strength, force or energy. ---
examples: She smiled weakly and closed her eyes.
The patient's heart was beating weakly.
"I'm fine," he said weakly.
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Weakly sounds exactly like weekly (еженедельно, раз в неделю).

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are very tired or tired of something. ---
examples: He climbed the stairs wearily.
She sighed wearily and sat down.
"Not again," he said wearily.
entries.position: end — also front (Wearily, she sat down)
entries.contrast: Do not mix up wearily (устало, from weary) and warily (настороженно, from wary).

entries.meaning: Every week, continuing for a long time. ---
examples: Week after week, the show topped the ratings.
She visited her father in the hospital week after week.
We ate the same meals week after week.
entries.type: frequency — every week for a long time
entries.position: front or end
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause
entries.form: the same pattern as day after day, year after year

entries.meaning: Weirdly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's been acting weirdly all week.
The streets were weirdly quiet for a Saturday night.
Weirdly, I wasn't hungry at all.
Weirdly enough, nobody noticed the mistake.

senses.head: In a strange or unusual way
examples: He's been acting weirdly all week.
The streets were weirdly quiet for a Saturday night.

senses.head: Surprisingly — commenting on a whole statement, often weirdly enough
examples: Weirdly, I wasn't hungry at all.
Weirdly enough, nobody noticed the mistake.

entries.position: any position — end for manner; before an adjective (weirdly quiet); front as a comment (Weirdly, …)

entries.meaning: Toward or in the west. ---
examples: We drove west across Kansas.
The windows face west, so the sunsets are amazing.
The lake is about thirty miles west of the city.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of motion, and be, live, lie
entries.form: flat — the same form as the noun and adjective west
entries.contrast: As an adverb it takes no preposition: drive west, head west, not drive to west. With the it is a noun: in the west, to the west of town. Out west is common in American speech for the western states: They moved out west.

entries.meaning: In addition, and more importantly. ---
examples: The hotel was cheap. What's more, it was right on the beach.
He's late again, and what is more, he didn't call.
The new phone is faster; what's more, the battery lasts two days.
entries.position: front — with a comma

entries.meaning: At all — used after a noun phrase to strengthen a negative. ---
examples: I have no interest whatsoever in politics.
There's no evidence whatsoever that it works.
Did he give any reason whatsoever?
entries.position: after its word — after a noun phrase with no or any
entries.contrast: Only in negatives, questions, and after any, and always after the noun phrase: no idea whatsoever, never ✗ whatsoever no idea. It is a stronger, more formal at all.

entries.meaning: In a playful, unusual and charming way. ---
examples: The café is whimsically decorated with old toys.
She named her cats whimsically, after famous poets.
The children's book is whimsically illustrated.
entries.position: end — or mid before a participle (whimsically decorated)

entries.meaning: Completely; used to stress how new or different something is. ---
examples: Having a baby is a whole new experience.
That's a whole different story.
Moving to Texas was a whole other adventure.
entries.type: degree — in a whole new, a whole different, a whole other
entries.position: before its word — between a and the adjective
entries.modifies: the adjectives new, different and other
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective whole
entries.contrast: In the whole day (целый день) and swallow it whole (целиком), whole is an adjective. The adverb only strengthens new, different or other after a: a whole new world means 'a completely new world', not 'a whole world that is new'.

entries.meaning: Completely and sincerely, with no doubts. ---
examples: I wholeheartedly agree with you.
We support the idea wholeheartedly.
She threw herself wholeheartedly into the new job.
entries.position: mid or end — I wholeheartedly agree, I agree wholeheartedly
entries.modifies: verbs of agreeing, supporting and committing

entries.meaning: Wholesale has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We buy our coffee beans wholesale.
The bakery sells wholesale to restaurants and hotels.
The committee rejected the proposal wholesale.
The new owner replaced the staff almost wholesale.

senses.head: In large amounts at a lower price, usually to be sold again
examples: We buy our coffee beans wholesale.
The bakery sells wholesale to restaurants and hotels.

senses.head: On a large scale, all at once, without picking out exceptions
examples: The committee rejected the proposal wholesale.
The new owner replaced the staff almost wholesale.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of buying and selling; verbs of rejecting, replacing and destroying
entries.form: flat — the same form as the noun and adjective wholesale

entries.meaning: Completely; entirely. ---
examples: I'm not wholly convinced by his story.
The company is wholly owned by the family.
That's a wholly different question.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and participles; mid before a verb
entries.contrast: Wholly is often pronounced just like holy (святой). It is formal; in speech completely or totally is more usual. Not wholly means 'not entirely' (не совсем).

entries.meaning: Wickedly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The show is wickedly funny.
It's a wickedly clever plan.
Her comments were short and wickedly smart.
He grinned wickedly and grabbed the last cookie.
The villain laughed wickedly.

senses.head: Very; extremely — about something clever or entertaining
examples: The show is wickedly funny.
It's a wickedly clever plan.
Her comments were short and wickedly smart.

senses.head: In a mischievous or evil way
examples: He grinned wickedly and grabbed the last cookie.
The villain laughed wickedly.

entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (wickedly funny); end for manner
entries.modifies: adjectives, mostly of good qualities (funny, smart, clever); verbs like grin and laugh

entries.meaning: Without control or supervision, in run wild. ---
examples: The kids ran wild while their parents talked.
Weeds are running wild in the backyard.
Don't let your imagination run wild.
entries.position: end — after run
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective wild
entries.contrast: Adverb wild lives mainly in the set phrase run wild. In go wild and drive someone wild it is an adjective. Everywhere else use wildly: She waved wildly, not waved wild.

entries.meaning: Wildly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The crowd cheered wildly.
She waved her arms wildly to get our attention.
The dog was barking wildly at the door.
The show was wildly popular in the '90s.
His guess was wildly inaccurate.
Prices vary wildly from store to store.

senses.head: In an uncontrolled, excited or violent way
examples: The crowd cheered wildly.
She waved her arms wildly to get our attention.
The dog was barking wildly at the door.

senses.head: Extremely; very far from what is normal or correct
examples: The show was wildly popular in the '90s.
His guess was wildly inaccurate.
Prices vary wildly from store to store.

entries.position: end — for manner; before its word for degree (wildly popular)
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives like popular, successful, inaccurate, different

entries.meaning: On purpose, knowing that it is wrong or harmful. ---
examples: He willfully ignored the doctor's advice.
The company willfully violated safety laws.
She was accused of willfully misleading investors.
entries.position: mid — before a verb or participle (willfully ignored)
entries.modifies: verbs of ignoring, violating and misleading

entries.meaning: Because you want to or are happy to, without being forced. ---
examples: She willingly gave up her weekend to help.
Nobody would willingly live next to a landfill.
He went with the officers willingly.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: Willy-nilly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't just throw your clothes in the drawer willy-nilly.
The city approved new buildings willy-nilly.
Money was being spent willy-nilly.
We were dragged into the argument willy-nilly.
Willy-nilly, the town had to accept the new factory.

senses.head: Carelessly and without a plan; haphazardly
examples: Don't just throw your clothes in the drawer willy-nilly.
The city approved new buildings willy-nilly.
Money was being spent willy-nilly.

senses.head: Whether you want to or not
examples: We were dragged into the argument willy-nilly.
Willy-nilly, the town had to accept the new factory.

entries.position: end
entries.form: rhyming compound, from old will I, nill I — 'whether I want or not'
entries.contrast: Russian волей-неволей matches only the older second sense. Most Americans use willy-nilly informally to mean 'haphazardly' (как попало), so They spent money willy-nilly is about carelessness, not about being forced.

entries.meaning: With good judgment; sensibly. ---
examples: Choose your friends wisely.
She wisely decided not to answer.
Spend your money wisely — it has to last all month.
entries.position: any position — end for manner; mid or front as a comment (She wisely said nothing)

entries.meaning: With a slightly sad longing for something you do not have or have lost. ---
examples: She looked wistfully at the old photos.
"I used to live there," he said wistfully.
The kids stared wistfully out the window at the snow.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of looking, smiling and speaking

entries.meaning: With scorn meant to make someone feel foolish or ashamed. ---
examples: She looked at him witheringly and walked away.
"Nice try," the teacher said witheringly.
The review was witheringly critical of the director.
entries.position: end — or before its word (witheringly critical)
entries.modifies: verbs of looking and speaking; adjectives of criticism

entries.meaning: Inside a building, a group or a person. ---
examples: Help wanted — inquire within.
Real change has to come from within.
The biggest threat was the enemy within.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs, mostly in set phrases: inquire within, from within, the enemy within
entries.contrast: Within is far more common as a preposition with a noun after it: within an hour (в течение часа), within the city limits (в пределах города). The adverb, with nothing after it, is formal and lives mainly in set phrases like inquire within on a shop sign.

entries.meaning: Certainly; with no reason to doubt it. ---
examples: This is without doubt the best pizza in town.
Without a doubt, she's the smartest person on the team.
He was the right choice, without doubt.
entries.position: front or end — or before its word (without doubt the best)
entries.modifies: a whole clause; a superlative phrase
entries.form: also without a doubt, more common in speech
entries.contrast: Without (a) doubt means certainly; no doubt is weaker and often means probably: No doubt he'll be late again (наверняка).

entries.meaning: In a clever and funny way. ---
examples: The speech was wittily written.
He answered the reporter's question wittily.
She wittily summed up the whole debate in one line.
entries.position: end — or mid before a participle (wittily written)
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking and writing; past participles

entries.meaning: Knowing what you are doing; on purpose. ---
examples: Wittingly or not, she helped the scammers.
He would never wittingly hurt anyone.
Many people wittingly or unwittingly share false stories online.
entries.position: mid — before the verb; often in wittingly or unwittingly
entries.contrast: Much rarer than its opposite unwittingly (невольно, по незнанию), and usually paired with it: wittingly or unwittingly.

entries.meaning: Very badly; to a sad or shameful degree. ---
examples: The hospital is woefully understaffed.
We were woefully unprepared for the storm.
The school's budget is woefully inadequate.
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: negative adjectives and participles: inadequate, unprepared, understaffed

entries.meaning: Very well; in a way that is very pleasing. ---
examples: The kids behaved wonderfully at dinner.
It's a wonderfully funny book.
Everything worked out wonderfully in the end.
entries.position: end — for manner; before its word as an intensifier (wonderfully warm)

entries.meaning: Stiffly, without natural feeling or expression. ---
examples: The actors delivered their lines woodenly.
He smiled woodenly for the cameras.
She read the statement woodenly, without looking up.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of acting, speaking and moving

entries.meaning: In exactly the same words. ---
examples: He copied the essay word for word from the internet.
Can you repeat what she said word for word?
Don't translate word for word; translate the meaning.
entries.type: manner — in exactly the same words
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without saying anything. ---
examples: She wordlessly handed him the letter.
He nodded wordlessly and left the room.
Wordlessly, they walked back to the car.
entries.position: any position — mid before the verb, end, or front with a comma

entries.meaning: Throughout the world. ---
examples: The film earned nine hundred million dollars worldwide.
The company now ships worldwide.
Millions of viewers worldwide watched the launch.
entries.position: end — or after a noun: fans worldwide
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective worldwide

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are worried. ---
examples: "Is she okay?" he asked worriedly.
Her mother kept glancing worriedly at the clock.
The pilot looked worriedly at the fuel gauge.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of asking, looking and speaking

entries.meaning: Unfairly or illegally. ---
examples: He spent twenty years in prison after being wrongfully convicted.
She sued the company, claiming she was wrongfully fired.
The family says their son was wrongfully arrested.
entries.position: mid — before a participle (wrongfully convicted)
entries.modifies: past participles and verbs of accusing, arresting, firing and convicting
entries.contrast: Wrongfully is about injustice or breaking the law: wrongfully convicted, wrongfully fired. For a simple mistake use wrongly or incorrectly: The name was spelled wrongly.

entries.meaning: With dry, slightly mocking humor.
examples: "Well, that went well," she said wryly.
He smiled wryly when he saw the mistake.
The book wryly describes life in a small office.
entries.position: end — or mid before the verb
entries.modifies: verbs of smiling, speaking and writing
